summary: Austria is a landlocked country in Central Europe, once the core of the Habsburg monarchy and Austria-Hungary, and is known for its Alpine scenery, classical music and café culture.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: From the 8th century Catholicism spread through the Alpine region with the missionary activity of the diocese of Salzburg, and in 798 Salzburg became an archdiocese. During the Reformation in the 16th century many Austrians converted to Protestantism for a time, but the Habsburgs promoted the Counter-Reformation and restored Catholicism through expulsion and forced conversion, making Austria a Catholic power. In recent years, because of secularization and tens of thousands of people leaving the Church each year (to avoid paying the church tax), the share has fallen from about nine tenths in 1951 to about half.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has increased rapidly since the 1970s, especially in cities such as Vienna. The causes include postwar secularization, rising levels of education, the church tax system (church members must pay about 1 percent of income), and waves of leaving the Church triggered by events such as the 1995 sexual abuse scandal of Cardinal Groër; in Vienna 'no religion' is already the largest category.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam has a special historical status in Austria: after Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia in 1908, the Islam Law was passed in 1912, formally recognizing Islam. Today's Muslims are mainly 'guest workers' who came from Turkey and Yugoslavia after the 1960s and their descendants, and migrants from Syria and Afghanistan during the 2015 refugee wave.

ranking.name: Orthodox Christianity
ranking.description: Most Orthodox believers are Serbs and Romanians who came to Austria as 'guest workers' in the 1960s and 70s, and their descendants. Vienna had been a city where Balkan merchants gathered since the Habsburg era, with Greek and Serbian Orthodox churches already in the 18th century, and today several Orthodox churches serve the immigrant communities.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism (mainly Lutheranism) once spread widely among Austrian nobles and peasants in the 16th century, but was suppressed during the Counter-Reformation and many believers were expelled, for example when the Archbishop of Salzburg expelled about twenty thousand Protestants in 1731. Only after Joseph II issued the Patent of Toleration in 1781 could Protestantism exist legally, but only a minority remains today, mainly in Carinthia and Burgenland.

religion.background: Christianity had already reached Austria in Roman times, and from the 8th century the dioceses of Salzburg and Passau were responsible for missionary work, so that Catholicism became the mainstream. The Reformation of the 16th century made Protestantism prevalent for a time, but the Habsburgs restored Catholicism through the Counter-Reformation, and from then on Catholicism was closely tied to imperial identity. Joseph II's Patent of Toleration of 1781 gave Protestants and Orthodox believers limited freedom, and the 1867 constitution further guaranteed religious freedom. After World War II, secularization and immigration gradually diversified the religious structure, and the Catholic share has continued to fall.

language.official: German is the official language of Austria, and in some regions Croatian, Slovenian and Hungarian are also recognized as regional official languages.

ranking.name: German (Austrian German)
ranking.description: German became the main language from the early Middle Ages when the Bavarians settled here; Austrian German differs from standard German in pronunciation and vocabulary, for example 'Jänner' (January) and 'Erdäpfel' (potatoes). After the collapse of Austria-Hungary in 1918, Austria became a small country with a predominantly German-speaking population, and about nine tenths of the population speak German as a mother tongue, with everyday speech mostly in Bavarian dialects.

ranking.name: Bosnian / Croatian / Serbian
ranking.description: Speakers of Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are mainly the 'guest workers' recruited from Yugoslavia in the 1960s and 70s and their families, and the refugees who fled to Austria during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s. In addition, the Croatian minority in Burgenland are descendants of people who moved north in the 16th century to escape the Ottoman wars, and their language is protected as a regional official language.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish speakers are mainly the Turkish workers who came to Austria after the labor recruitment agreement between Austria and Turkey was signed in 1964, and their descendants. The workers, who were originally expected to work for a short time, mostly settled and brought their families, forming sizable Turkish communities in Vienna, Upper Austria and elsewhere.

language.history: From the 6th century the Bavarians entered the area of present-day Austria and settled, bringing the dialects that later developed into Austrian German. From the Middle Ages to the 19th century the Habsburgs ruled a multi-ethnic empire; the Vienna court used German, but more than ten languages, including Czech, Hungarian, Polish and Croatian, were used within the empire. After the empire collapsed in 1918, Austria became a German-speaking country, and the 1955 Austrian State Treaty guaranteed the language rights of the Slovenian and Croatian minorities. The labor migration wave after the 1960s and the refugee wave of the 1990s brought large numbers of speakers of Balkan languages and Turkish.

ranking.name: Wiener Schnitzel
ranking.description: Veal slices are pounded thin, coated with flour, egg and breadcrumbs and fried in butter or lard into a thin, golden, crisp cutlet, served with lemon wedges and potato salad.
ranking.history: The origin of Wiener Schnitzel is much debated; the most widespread story is that in 1857 the Austrian field marshal Radetzky brought the breaded cutlet from Milan, Italy, to Vienna, but historians consider this a 20th-century legend, because earlier Austrian recipes already contain breaded fried dishes. Under Austrian law, only one made with veal may be called 'Wiener Schnitzel', and one made with pork must be labeled 'Viennese style'. It is Austria's most representative national dish.

ranking.name: Sachertorte
ranking.description: A rich chocolate sponge cake with a layer of apricot jam, coated with a glossy dark chocolate glaze, usually served with unsweetened whipped cream.
ranking.history: The Sachertorte was made in 1832 by the 16-year-old apprentice Franz Sacher for a banquet of the Austrian chancellor Metternich; later his son Eduard perfected the recipe at the Demel pastry shop in Vienna and in 1876 founded the Hotel Sacher. In the mid-20th century the Hotel Sacher and Demel fought a lawsuit for years over who could use the name 'original Sachertorte', and in the end the Hotel Sacher won the designation 'Original'. 5 December is designated National Sachertorte Day.

ranking.name: Apfelstrudel
ranking.description: Paper-thin dough is rolled around apple slices, raisins, cinnamon, sugar and toasted breadcrumbs and baked, then sliced and dusted with powdered sugar, often served with vanilla sauce.
ranking.history: The pastry technique of strudel is generally thought to derive from the layered phyllo dough of the Ottoman Empire (as in baklava) and to have entered the Habsburg lands via Hungary in the 16th and 17th centuries. The earliest surviving apple strudel recipe is a 1696 manuscript from Vienna, kept in the Vienna City Library. In the Habsburg era it became a classic dessert of Viennese cafés and is still one of Austria's most popular desserts today.

ranking.name: Tafelspitz
ranking.description: Beef rump is gently simmered with root vegetables; the clear broth is drunk first and then the sliced beef is eaten, served with apple-horseradish sauce and chive sauce.
ranking.history: Tafelspitz is a classic dish of the Viennese court and middle-class households, and in the 19th century it became famous because the Austrian emperor Franz Joseph I ate it every day for lunch. The dish reflects the Viennese tradition of being particular about cuts of beef, and butchers could distinguish dozens of different cuts. Today Vienna still has old restaurants that specialize in Tafelspitz, and it is a representative dish of the locals' Sunday family meals.

ranking.name: Kaiserschmarrn
ranking.description: A thick pancake made from eggs, flour and milk, torn into small pieces with a fork after frying, dusted with powdered sugar and eaten with plum compote or apple sauce.
ranking.history: The name 'Kaiserschmarrn' is associated with Franz Joseph I, and the story that circulates is that in the 19th century, when the emperor was in the Alpine region, the cook fried the pancake so that it fell apart and had to tear it up to serve it, and the emperor liked it. However, these stories are hard to verify. It was originally a simple meal of Alpine farmers and later became popular at the Habsburg court; today it is the most common dessert at Austrian mountain huts and ski resort restaurants.
